title: Call me bitter (Ruth 1:1–21)
hook: Naomi loses husband and sons in Moab and asks to be called Mara, bitter
carry: stay beside them, let their words stand
tomorrow: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ketuvim, the Writings, opened in human voices. Your line was they praise, they doubt, they complain. Today, the first story on the Talmud's list.

Two women walk into Bethlehem, dusty from the road, and the whole town comes out to look. In the King James, "all the city was moved about them, and they said, Is this Naomi?" She left with a husband and two sons. She's come back with none of them, and the woman beside her is a foreigner from Moab. The neighbors aren't cruel. They're just shocked; they can barely match the face they knew to the one in front of them. And Naomi answers in a way nobody expects. She tells them to stop using her name.
screen: `TWO WOMEN WALK INTO BETHLEHEM.` → `IS THIS NAOMI?` → `STOP USING MY NAME.`

segments.voice: Go back to how the book begins: "in the days when the judges ruled," a famine in the land. A man of Bethlehem, Elimelech, takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to the fields of Moab to survive. There Elimelech dies. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons die. The King James puts it in one bare line: "the woman was left of her two sons and her husband." Left. That's the word for her. When she hears there's bread again at home, she sets out, and on the road she begs her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah, weeping, goes. Ruth won't. That moment is tomorrow's. Today belongs to Naomi at the city gate. "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Mara means bitter. Then: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Notice three things. First, she says it out loud, in public, and she says it about God; she doesn't pretend to be fine for the neighbors. Second, the book doesn't correct her. No one tells her to look on the bright side, and her words are kept, exactly as she said them, in Scripture. Third, the quiet ache: when Naomi says empty, Ruth is standing right next to her, the one person who stayed. Grief that deep can't see it yet, and the story doesn't rush her. It only adds that they arrived at the beginning of barley harvest.
screen: `A FAMINE, MOAB, AND THREE GRAVES.` · `THE WOMAN WAS LEFT.` · then, large: `CALL ME NOT NAOMI, CALL ME MARA.` · then: `SHE SAYS EMPTY, AND RUTH IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying a heavy loss, a death, a divorce, a home, a job, a body that doesn't work the way it did. Don't fix it or find the bright side for them; in your mind, just stand beside them at the gate, saying nothing, staying, the way the book lets Naomi be. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words.
Mara. Hebrew for bitter, the name Naomi asks to be called, and the book lets her say it. Today's word.
Your line: stay beside them, let their words stand. The book keeps Naomi's words. That's day eight hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: The book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot, and Jews count it among the short scrolls of the Writings.
